Stefano Forli, PhD: The Forli Lab uses computer-based methods to help design new medicines. Rather than testing molecules only in a wet lab, the team builds computational models of proteins and other biological molecules to find "druggable" pockets where a drug could bind and change how the protein works. They use techniques like molecular dynamics simulations, homology modeling, and molecular docking to predict how small molecules interact with these targets, then screen large virtual libraries of compounds (high-throughput virtual screening) or design custom compound libraries to find promising drug candidates. The lab also builds and freely distributes AutoDock, a widely used software suite for docking small molecules and peptides against proteins and nucleic acids. This combination of tool-building and drug discovery aims to speed the path from basic biology to new therapies.
Martin Friedlander, MD, PhD: The Friedlander Lab studies eye diseases that damage the retina, focusing especially on a condition called macular telangiectasia (MacTel), which causes vision loss. The lab's work identified gene mutations that stop MacTel patients from making enough of an amino acid the eye needs, helping explain why the disease develops. Building on this, the group and collaborators helped develop and test a cell-based therapy (ENCELTO) in a Phase 3 clinical trial, supporting its FDA approval as the first cell-based treatment for MacTel. The lab has also studied stem cells as a way to protect or restore vision, and found that restoring a naturally occurring compound called erucamide in the eye stabilized retinal tissue in preclinical models of retinal degeneration. Together, this research spans discovering disease causes to developing and testing new treatments for blinding retinal conditions.
John Griffin, PhD: The Griffin Lab studies the biology of blood-clotting proteins and how they protect cells beyond their classic role in coagulation. Their published research shows that activated protein C, a natural blood protein, can prevent programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the cells lining blood vessels, acting through specific cell-surface receptors. This cell-protective, anti-inflammatory activity has led the lab toward new applications: a drug candidate developed over the last decade, originally aimed at easing inflammation and protecting blood vessels, is now also being explored as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease by protecting brain cells from damage. The lab's broader work has also pointed to potential new approaches for treating cardiovascular disease. Overall, the group works at the intersection of blood biology, inflammation, and neuroprotection to find new therapeutic strategies for vascular and neurodegenerative conditions.
Danielle Grotjahn, PhD: The Grotjahn Lab studies mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing organelles, which the lab has shown also act as sensors of cellular stress. Using advanced imaging tools -- particularly cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and super-resolution fluorescence microscopy -- the team visualizes mitochondria in unprecedented detail inside intact cells, connecting their molecular structure to their function. Their work has revealed how mitochondria change shape in response to genetic and environmental stress, how ribosomes attached to mitochondria alter the local membrane environment for protein import, and a new way to measure membrane thickness directly inside cells. They have also studied how DNA, magnesium, and polyphosphate interact to organize genetic material. This research aims to uncover fundamental mechanisms of mitochondrial adaptation that could inform new therapies for diseases where mitochondria are disrupted, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and cancer.
Howard Hang, PhD: The Hang Lab studies how chemical signals from microbes -- especially gut bacteria -- communicate with human cells to shape immunity and health. Many of these signaling molecules, called metabolites, come from the body's own metabolism or from diet, the microbiome, and medications, and have been hard to study mechanistically. To understand them, the lab develops chemical methods to characterize how metabolites interact with proteins, and uses animal models to discover protective factors made by specific gut bacteria species and figure out how they work. This approach has revealed new functions for metabolites in immunity and in microbial disease-causing mechanisms, as well as new protective factors from the microbiome. One finding: disabling a single bacterial protein can restore the antibiotic vancomycin's power against resistant bacteria. The lab's discoveries are generating new therapeutic leads and biomarkers for infection, inflammation, and immunotherapy.
Mia L. Huang, PhD: The Huang Lab studies glycans -- complex sugar molecules that coat the surface of cells and act as signals directing important biological processes like tissue communication, growth, and immune activation. Because glycans are structurally complex, they have historically been difficult to study, so the lab develops chemical tools to decode their function. The team combines synthetic chemistry, mass spectrometry, and protein engineering to investigate how glycans influence stem cell differentiation, musculoskeletal biology, and cancer. In one line of research, the lab identified a molecule called galectin-3 that binds sugar molecules on cell-surface proteins and helps hold placental cells together as they fuse during early pregnancy -- a process that, when it fails, can lead to complications like preeclampsia. This work is helping guide new ways to diagnose or treat conditions such as cancer, liver disease, and pregnancy complications.
Darrell Irvine, PhD: The Irvine Lab engineers new ways to direct the immune system against disease, combining principles from immunology with biotechnology and materials chemistry. The lab designs synthetic materials -- including nanotechnology and "smart" biomaterials -- to make vaccines more effective and to strengthen the immune system's attack on tumors. A major focus is vaccine development for HIV and for cancer immunotherapy: the team has designed DNA scaffolds that carry HIV vaccine proteins into the body to sharpen the immune response, and has tested vaccine regimens in non-human primates that generated antibodies capable of neutralizing multiple HIV strains, a first for the field. Beyond HIV, the lab's engineering approaches are applied broadly to infectious disease, cancer, and autoimmune conditions, aiming to translate fundamental immunology and materials science into practical vaccines and immunotherapies for hard-to-treat diseases.
Kim Janda, PhD: The Janda Lab develops vaccines and antibody-based treatments to counter opioid and synthetic drug overdoses. The team has created a vaccine that trains the immune system to rapidly neutralize fentanyl and newer synthetic fentanyl analogs, and an early proof-of-concept vaccine aimed at treating overdose from xylazine, an animal sedative increasingly mixed into street drugs. They have also developed a biologic (antibody-based treatment) that works against carfentanil, an extremely potent synthetic opioid, and shown in preclinical studies that a human antibody targeting carfentanil and fentanyl can reverse overdose effects. In related work, the lab modified an opioid-like molecule to reduce respiratory depression -- the main cause of opioid overdose deaths -- while keeping its pain-blocking effects. This vaccine- and antibody-based approach to blocking drugs before they reach the brain represents a new strategy for reducing overdose deaths.
Xin Jin, PhD: The Jin Lab studies the brain using neuroscience and genomics, with a focus on how genes shape brain development. Jin's research maps the genes and cell types involved in brain development, work recognized by a McKnight Scholar Award and a 2024 Pew Scholar award. The lab has also received major funding to study interoception, the body's ability to sense its own internal state -- sometimes described as a "sixth sense" -- as part of a $14.2 million effort to map this system in humans. Separately, the lab is investigating how environmental pollution may contribute to autism risk and how specific genes raise the risk of psychiatric disorders. Together, this work aims to connect genetics, brain circuitry, and environmental factors to better understand both healthy brain development and the origins of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.
